A loan is listed when its borrower's name equals the name of an organization in the City's nonprofit-spending table, or the legal name on that organization's tax returns, once capital letters, punctuation, “Inc” and common abbreviations are set aside, and the organization's matched loans come to $150,000 or more. That gives 242 loans to the case's 179 organizations: $264,090,743 lent and $260,384,093 forgiven. The case says $265.0 million lent and $261,320,430 forgiven; the difference is $924,463 lent and $936,342 forgiven. Loan 4317557209 is one loan that the case counts twice, under Asian & Pacific Islander Wellness Center and under San Francisco Community Health Center: the federal extract matched it to both City payee names, which carry one employer identification number (94-3096109). It is listed here once. 158 organizations were matched on the City's name and 21 on the legal name from tax returns. As a second check, each loan's street number and ZIP code were compared with the addresses on the tax returns collected for the payee: they agree for 153 organizations and not for 26, which are listed separately. 1 of the loans shows no amount forgiven in the file.
tables.limits: A Paycheck Protection Program loan was a federal loan for payroll that was forgiven when the borrower kept its staff; taking one and having it forgiven was what the program was for. The amount forgiven is often slightly more than the amount lent; the file does not say why, and interest that built up before forgiveness would explain it. The number of jobs is the borrower's own statement. The federal file carries no tax identification number, so a borrower is tied to a City payee by its name. Near matches were left out, so a borrower that spelled its name differently is missing, and an unrelated business with exactly the same name could be included. The loan file was matched against every San Francisco borrower, not only those marked nonprofit: for 27 organizations the file records the borrower's kind of business as something other than a nonprofit (a corporation, a professional association, a sole proprietorship), which may be how the form was filled in or may mean a different business of the same name. Nothing here shows that a salary paid by a forgiven loan was also billed to the City: that would show only in contract invoices, which are not public.

tables.how: The 179 organizations of the case, largest loans first, with the figures the case uses: loans of $265,015,206 in all and $261,320,434 forgiven (the case's $265.0 million and $261,320,430), and City payments from the Controller's nonprofit-spending table. An organization is counted as rising when its fiscal 2021 payments are at least 1.1 times its fiscal 2019 payments and fiscal 2019 is above zero: 87 organizations. 10 more had no payment in fiscal 2019 and some in fiscal 2021 and are not counted among them. By the Controller's table of every payment, 82 of the 87 also rose by 10% or more. 2 of the 179 had no City payment in either table until after fiscal 2021, so they were not City-funded when they borrowed: Raphael House of San Francisco, Inc (first paid in fiscal 2026); SF Bicycle Coalition Education Fund (first paid in fiscal 2024). Loan 4317557209 is one loan that the case counts twice, under Asian & Pacific Islander Wellness Center and under San Francisco Community Health Center: the federal extract matched it to both City payee names, which carry one employer identification number (94-3096109). Both names are rows here, so this list adds to the case’s figure and the list of loans to the smaller one.
tables.limits: A rise in City payments does not show that the loan was not needed: the City is often a small part of an organization's income, and ticket sales, fees and donations fell in 2020 even where City grants grew. City payments include money an organization pays onward as rent subsidies or grants to others. The two Controller tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment. A Paycheck Protection Program loan was a federal loan for payroll that was forgiven when the borrower kept its staff; taking one and having it forgiven was what the program was for. The amount forgiven is often slightly more than the amount lent; the file does not say why, and interest that built up before forgiveness would explain it. The number of jobs is the borrower's own statement. The federal file carries no tax identification number, so a borrower is tied to a City payee by its name.

tables.how: Every payment to the 179 organizations in fiscal 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022, the years around the loans (approved from 4 April 2020 to 28 May 2021). The case's figures come from the first of the two tables. 2 organizations have no row because neither table shows a payment to them in those four years: Raphael House of San Francisco, Inc (first paid in fiscal 2026); SF Bicycle Coalition Education Fund (first paid in fiscal 2024). Each organization's payments in the two tables the Controller publishes, as retrieved on 12 November 2026: Citywide Nonprofit Spending, which by its own description keeps contracted services only, and Vendor Payments (Vouchers), the table of every payment. The fiscal year is the one printed on the payment. Payee names are matched by the rule the organization pages use: the name without punctuation and company suffixes, plus the renames and spellings that a shared contract number confirms.
tables.limits: These rows show whose City money was rising; they do not show what any payment was for or whether a cost was also covered by a federal loan. A payment is money the City sent, not money the organization kept or spent on itself: subsidies, rent aid and grants that an organization pays on to others are in these figures. The two tables differ where the nonprofit-spending table leaves out a kind of payment or a contract; neither is wrong for that reason. The year printed on a payment can be later than the year the payment was issued. A payee the City spells in a way that no contract number ties to the organization is not counted.

tables.how: Every match in this case begins with the name, because the federal loan file carries no tax identification number. For 153 of the 179 organizations a second fact agrees: the street number and ZIP code on a loan are those on a tax return collected for the payee. These 26 are the rest, with the address the loan file gives and the addresses the returns give. Together they account for $54,521,902 of the forgiven amount.
tables.limits: A different address is ordinary: an organization can borrow from an office, a post-office box or a new address that its tax return does not show, and several of these names are distinctive enough that a second organization of the same name in San Francisco is unlikely. The row says only that the match was not confirmed by a second fact. The tax returns were themselves tied to the City payee by name.
